content.text:
You're right, and the code makes it sharper than "still representing a lock."

`VirtualLock` is dispatched on platform `"virtual"` — the hass-virtual custom integration — which creates a genuine `lock` domain entity. It has lock/unlock state, HA exposes lock/unlock services for it, and the tests drive it (`async_set(entity_id, "locked")`). LCM never actuates it, but "LCM doesn't use that half" isn't the same as "that half doesn't exist."

The decisive bit is what the provider says about itself:

```python
@property
def supports_code_slot_events(self) -> bool:
    """
    Return False: a virtual lock observes nothing.

    It is a recording surface -- somewhere to point a use that happened
    beyond Home Assistant's reach -- rather than a device that reports one.
    """
```

A keypad is *exactly* a thing that observes credential entry. This provider explicitly returns `False` for that. So against #1480's own three-role table:

| Role | `VirtualLock` |
|---|---|
| credential **store** | yes — its `Store` |
| credential **entry point** | **no** — observes nothing, by design |
| **actuated** thing | yes, a real lock entity; LCM just never drives it |

`VirtualKeypad` would name it after the single role it explicitly disclaims, and un-name the one role it genuinely has. The old note in #1480 said the rename "names the recording surface well" — that was wrong. A recording surface is where a use is *pointed*, not where it's *entered*; the entry point is the ESPHome keypad, which is the `source` on the event and isn't this provider at all.

So: **don't rename.** `VirtualLock` is accurate — it's a virtual lock that happens to be the credential store too. The store-not-device nature is already carried by the docstrings, the README row, and the wiki page, which is the right place for it.

## Proposed change

Closes out #1480: **a provider is a credential store, not a lock.**

The headline change is that an entry can now manage **no locks at all**. Credentials live in the entry's configuration and are checked with `lock_code_manager.use_credential`, which is what a keypad Lock Code Manager cannot talk to actually needs — an entry to check credentials *against*, not a lock to write them *to*. That's issue #1414 (ESPHome keypads) and #1484.

Two designs were built and dropped on the way: a reader provider, then codeless-lock declarations (#1489). Both tried to give the keypad a lock-shaped identity. The working version doesn't: validation already reads the entry's own configuration, so the only thing standing in the way was availability being `any()` over the lock roster. The feature is a five-line guard.

### What's in it

- **#1485** — `build_lock_instance` receives the config entry.
- **#1486 / #1500** — a per-member declaration shape, added for codeless locks and removed once that design was dropped. Net zero; they cancel out.
- **#1487** — `event_types` becomes credential kinds, `source`/`target` move into attributes. Landed atomically with all four dependents: the websocket last-used lookup, both usage blueprints, and `calendar_condition.yaml`.
- **#1492 / #1496** — `use_credential` gained a lock-entity lookup, then had it reverted. With no lock required, the only entities a caller could name are native locks — exactly the ones that don't need the action. `config_entry_id` and `config_entry_title` (both shipped in 5.2.0) are unchanged.
- **#1496** — lock-less entries.
- **#1499** — the credential-used entity no longer follows lock availability, so a use reported while every lock is down still reaches consumers; and the Slot Usage Limiter no longer decrements on lock recovery or after a restart.

### User-visible changes

- An entry may be created with no locks selected.
- **Lock-by-code uses now record.** The old `to == unlocked` filter is gone, so a credential that *locked* the door reaches the event entity. The limiter's `counted_operations` input decides whether that spends a use; it counts `unlock` and `unknown` by default, so a guest locking up behind themselves doesn't burn a code.
- `calendar_condition.yaml` no longer exposes `lock_entity_ids`; the blueprint documents the removal.

### Not in it

`lock_code_manager_lock_state_changed` still fires. Retiring it is deferred to the next major version and is the only item left open on #1480.

- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

content.content:
=== External-Keypads.md (     241 lines) ===
# External Keypads and Code Readers

Lock Code Manager can check a code entered somewhere it doesn't control — an
ESPHome keypad, a Wiegand reader, an intercom — against the users, PINs and
conditions you already configured, and record that the credential was used.

Because the check runs against the same users driving your real locks, one PIN
and one schedule cover both. Disable a user and their code stops working at the
keypad too.

Lock Code Manager never opens anything. It answers, records, and fires an event;
what happens next is yours.

## The action

```yaml
- action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
  data:
    config_entry_title: House Locks   # or config_entry_id
    code: "{{ entered_code }}"
    source: sensor.keypad_code        # where the code was entered
    target: lock.garage               # what it was used against
  response_variable: check
```

| Response | Value |
|---|---|
| `valid` | `true` / `false` |
| `user` | the user's name when valid, else `null` |
| `reason` | `unknown_code`, `user_disabled`, or `condition_not_met` when invalid |

`source` and `target` are both required and may be any entity. If you have no
natural entity for one, use a template entity as the source and a
[Virtual](https://github.com/twrecked/hass-virtual) lock as the target — see
[[Virtual integration|Virtual-integration]]. A keypad-only setup needs a Virtual
lock anyway, since a config entry requires at least one lock.

> **Don't name the same entity as both.** A use where `source` and `target` are
> equal is treated as one the lock observed by itself, and is not recorded again.

`reason` distinguishes a real-but-inactive credential from an unknown one, and
the action does no rate limiting or logging — so don't wire it to untrusted
input.

## What a valid code produces

**The `lock_code_manager_credential_used` event**, always:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `name` | the user |
| `config_entry_id`, `config_entry_title` | which configuration |
| `source` | where entered |
| `target` | what it was used against |

The same event fires when one of your locks reports a code used at its own
keypad, so a single trigger covers both.

**The user's `credential_used` event entity**, when `target` is a lock in that
config entry that can record events. Otherwise only the event fires — which is
normal for a keypad opening something LCM doesn't manage.

An invalid code produces nothing.

## Act on it

Import the **Credential Used** blueprint (see [[Blueprints]]): trigger on a
credential use, optionally filter by configuration, users, sources or targets,
and supply whatever actions you like — unlock a door, open a cover, start a
vacuum. Lock Code Manager needs to know nothing about what you're driving.

By hand:

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Garage: open on a valid keypad code"
    triggers:
      - trigger: event
        event_type: lock_code_manager_credential_used
        event_data:
          source: sensor.keypad_code
    actions:
      - action: cover.open_cover
        target: {entity_id: cover.garage_door}
```

## Security: keep the code out of your history

A keypad that publishes entered codes to an entity puts a cleartext PIN in that
entity's state, and the recorder keeps state history. Exclude it:

```yaml
recorder:
  exclude:
    entities:
      - sensor.keypad_code
```

Lock Code Manager never publishes that entity's state — only its entity ID. The
recorder is the one place it can't help, because the entity belongs to the
integration that publishes it.

Recipe 2 below avoids the entity entirely, which is the most private option.

---

# Recipes

### 1. Keypad entity → validate → open

On the device, publish the code and clear it (clearing is what lets the same
code be entered twice in a row):

```yaml
key_collector:
  - id: pin_collector
    source_id: keypad
    min_length: 4
    max_length: 8
    end_keys: "#"
    end_key_required: true
    on_result:
      - text_sensor.template.publish:
          id: keypad_code
          state: !lambda 'return x;'
      - delay: 1s
      - text_sensor.template.publish: {id: keypad_code, state: ""}
```

In Home Assistant:

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Garage: check keypad codes"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: sensor.keypad_code
        not_to: [unknown, unavailable, ""]
    actions:
      - action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
        data:
          config_entry_title: House Locks
          code: "{{ trigger.to_state.state }}"
          source: sensor.keypad_code
          target: lock.garage
        response_variable: check
      - if: "{{ check.valid }}"
        then:
          - action: cover.open_cover
            target: {entity_id: cover.garage_door}
```

> `not_to: [unknown, unavailable, ""]` is **not optional** — without it, a Wi-Fi
> reconnect that republishes the device's last value runs this with nobody at the
> keypad.

### 2. Let the keypad ask for itself

ESPHome 2025.10+ can capture an action's response, so the device decides locally
and the code never becomes an entity state at all.

```yaml
    on_result:
      - homeassistant.action:
          action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
          data_template:
            config_entry_title: House Locks
            code: "{{ entered }}"
            source: binary_sensor.garage_keypad_status
            target: lock.garage
          variables:
            entered: !lambda 'return x;'
          capture_response: true
          on_success:
            - if:
                condition:
                  lambda: 'return response["valid"].as<bool>();'
                then:
                  - switch.turn_on: garage_relay
                  - rtttl.play: "ok:d=4,o=5,b=100:c6"
                else:
                  - rtttl.play: "no:d=4,o=5,b=100:c4,c4"
```

`source` still has to name an entity — any entity belonging to the keypad will
do.

### 3. Different feedback per rejection reason


=== External-Keypads.md (     241 lines) ===
# External Keypads and Code Readers

Lock Code Manager can check a code entered somewhere it doesn't control — an
ESPHome keypad, a Wiegand reader, an intercom — against the users, PINs and
conditions you already configured, and record that the credential was used.

Because the check runs against the same users driving your real locks, one PIN
and one schedule cover both. Disable a user and their code stops working at the
keypad too.

Lock Code Manager never opens anything. It answers, records, and fires an event;
what happens next is yours.

## The action

```yaml
- action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
  data:
    config_entry_title: House Locks   # or config_entry_id
    code: "{{ entered_code }}"
    source: sensor.keypad_code        # where the code was entered
    target: lock.garage               # what it was used against
  response_variable: check
```

| Response | Value |
|---|---|
| `valid` | `true` / `false` |
| `user` | the user's name when valid, else `null` |
| `reason` | `unknown_code`, `user_disabled`, or `condition_not_met` when invalid |

`source` and `target` are both required and may be any entity. If you have no
natural entity for one, use a template entity as the source and a
[Virtual](https://github.com/twrecked/hass-virtual) lock as the target — see
[[Virtual integration|Virtual-integration]]. A keypad-only setup needs a Virtual
lock anyway, since a config entry requires at least one lock.

> **Don't name the same entity as both.** A use where `source` and `target` are
> equal is treated as one the lock observed by itself, and is not recorded again.

`reason` distinguishes a real-but-inactive credential from an unknown one, and
the action does no rate limiting or logging — so don't wire it to untrusted
input.

## What a valid code produces

**The `lock_code_manager_credential_used` event**, always:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `name` | the user |
| `config_entry_id`, `config_entry_title` | which configuration |
| `source` | where entered |
| `target` | what it was used against |

The same event fires when one of your locks reports a code used at its own
keypad, so a single trigger covers both.

**The user's `credential_used` event entity**, when `target` is a lock in that
config entry that can record events. Otherwise only the event fires — which is
normal for a keypad opening something LCM doesn't manage.

An invalid code produces nothing.

## Act on it

Import the **Credential Used** blueprint (see [[Blueprints]]): trigger on a
credential use, optionally filter by configuration, users, sources or targets,
and supply whatever actions you like — unlock a door, open a cover, start a
vacuum. Lock Code Manager needs to know nothing about what you're driving.

By hand:

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Garage: open on a valid keypad code"
    triggers:
      - trigger: event
        event_type: lock_code_manager_credential_used
        event_data:
          source: sensor.keypad_code
    actions:
      - action: cover.open_cover
        target: {entity_id: cover.garage_door}
```

## Security: keep the code out of your history

A keypad that publishes entered codes to an entity puts a cleartext PIN in that
entity's state, and the recorder keeps state history. Exclude it:

```yaml
recorder:
  exclude:
    entities:
      - sensor.keypad_code
```

Lock Code Manager never publishes that entity's state — only its entity ID. The
recorder is the one place it can't help, because the entity belongs to the
integration that publishes it.

Recipe 2 below avoids the entity entirely, which is the most private option.

---

# Recipes

### 1. Keypad entity → validate → open

On the device, publish the code and clear it (clearing is what lets the same
code be entered twice in a row):

```yaml
key_collector:
  - id: pin_collector
    source_id: keypad
    min_length: 4
    max_length: 8
    end_keys: "#"
    end_key_required: true
    on_result:
      - text_sensor.template.publish:
          id: keypad_code
          state: !lambda 'return x;'
      - delay: 1s
      - text_sensor.template.publish: {id: keypad_code, state: ""}
```

In Home Assistant:

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Garage: check keypad codes"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: sensor.keypad_code
        not_to: [unknown, unavailable, ""]
    actions:
      - action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
        data:
          config_entry_title: House Locks
          code: "{{ trigger.to_state.state }}"
          source: sensor.keypad_code
          target: lock.garage
        response_variable: check
      - if: "{{ check.valid }}"
        then:
          - action: cover.open_cover
            target: {entity_id: cover.garage_door}
```

content.content:
The [Virtual](https://github.com/twrecked/hass-virtual) integration allows users to set up "virtual" entities of different types. One of those entity types is locks.

The reason support for this integration was added is because it can be used to test Lock Code Manager functionality without affecting your main locks. Because Virtual locks don't have support for setting and clearing user codes, the way this works is that user codes are persisted to disk as you set them. If you remove a Virtual lock from your configuration, the file will be removed to keep your file system clean.

If you are curious about Lock Code Manager and don't want to impact any existing locks functionality, I would encourage you to try setting up Lock Code Manager with Virtual locks first!

PS - the way Virtual locks integrate with LCM is not set in stone. If you have ideas on how to make support for these locks better, please open an issue.

## Anchoring a keypad-only setup

Virtual locks have a second use beyond trying things out. If you check codes
from an external keypad with `lock_code_manager.use_credential` and have no real
lock, add a Virtual lock to the config entry: it gives the entry slot capacity to
allocate against, somewhere for users and PINs to live, and an entity to name as
the `target` so uses are recorded on each user's credential used entity. See
[[External Keypads|External-Keypads]].

content.subject: Fix #1491: reauth orphans a dropped lock's credential store
content.description: Reauth calls async_update_entry + async_reload, so a lock swapped out never gets the per-lock removal the options flow does: invoke_lock_removed_handlers, lock_dropped repair deletion, and async_unload_lock(remove_permanently=True). For VirtualLock the store IS the credentials, so a cleartext PIN outlives every entry referencing it. Repro test lands in tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py::TestReauthLockSwap. Fix must SHARE the listener's removal block, not duplicate it — a second path would skip the repair deletion exactly like the sibling-method bug. Note async_unload_lock no-ops when the lock instance is absent (runtime_data.locks.pop -> continue), which matters if the entry failed setup.

## Slot Usage Limiter

[![Import Blueprint](https://my.home-assistant.io/badges/blueprint_import.svg)](https://my.home-assistant.io/redirect/blueprint_import/?blueprint_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Framan325%2Flock_code_manager%2Fblob%2Fmain%2Fblueprints%2Fautomation%2Flock_code_manager%2Fslot_usage_limiter.yaml)

**Type:** Automation

Decrements an `input_number` helper each time a code slot PIN is used. When the counter reaches 0, the slot is automatically disabled. Optionally resets the counter when the slot is re-enabled.

### Setup

1. Create an `input_number` helper (Settings → Devices & Services → Helpers) with min=0, max=your desired limit, and step=1.
2. Import this blueprint using the button above.
3. Create a new automation from the blueprint and configure it with your LCM config entry, slot number, and the helper you created.

### Inputs

| Input | Description | Default |
|-------|-------------|---------|
| **Lock Code Manager config entry** | The LCM config entry that manages your lock(s). | *(required)* |
| **Code slot number** | The code slot number to monitor (1–999). | *(required)* |
| **Uses counter** | An `input_number` helper that tracks remaining uses. | *(required)* |
| **Initial uses on re-enable** | When > 0, the counter resets to this value each time the slot is re-enabled. Set to 0 to disable auto-reset. | `0` |

> **Note:** This blueprint replaces the built-in *Number of Uses* feature (removed in 2.0) with an `input_number`-based approach. It provides external visibility into the remaining count and allows programmatic reset via automations or the UI.

content.content:
# Services and Actions

Lock Code Manager registers nine services (now called **actions** in modern Home Assistant). Seven act on a lock or a config entry directly; two are pure helpers that return data (a generated PIN, a deobfuscated log).

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`lock_code_manager.add_user`](#add_user) | Add a user to a config entry, on a slot number chosen by reading the locks. |
| [`lock_code_manager.delete_user`](#delete_user) | Remove a user, clearing their credential from the locks by default. |
| [`lock_code_manager.set_usercode`](#set_usercode) | Write a PIN to a single slot on a managed lock, bypassing slot configuration. |
| [`lock_code_manager.clear_usercode`](#clear_usercode) | Clear a single slot on a managed lock, bypassing slot configuration. |
| [`lock_code_manager.set_slot_condition`](#set_slot_condition) | Attach a condition entity (calendar, schedule, etc.) to a slot. |
| [`lock_code_manager.clear_slot_condition`](#clear_slot_condition) | Remove the condition entity from a slot. |
| [`lock_code_manager.hard_refresh_usercodes`](#hard_refresh_usercodes) | Re-query the lock for all stored PINs (provider-dependent). |
| [`lock_code_manager.generate_pin`](#generate_pin) | Return a cryptographically random PIN that passes safety filtering. |
| [`lock_code_manager.deobfuscate_log`](#deobfuscate_log) | Reverse `pin#xxxxxxxx` tokens in pasted log text back to plaintext PINs for local debugging. |

> **Tip:** All actions are also exposed in the UI's *Developer Tools → Actions* tab with full schema validation and help text.

---

## add_user

Add a user to a config entry. You name the person; Lock Code Manager picks the slot number, by reading what each lock actually holds and asking each provider where its slot numbers stop. Everybody already configured keeps the number they have.

This is the action behind the **Add user** card on the generated dashboard.
...
## generate_pin

# Adding and Removing Locks

Each Lock Code Manager config entry manages a set of locks and a set of users. The user configuration applies to **every** lock in the entry, so adding or removing a lock changes which locks the entry's users are synced to — it does not change the user configuration itself.

All of the flows below start from **Settings → Devices & Services → Lock Code Manager**, then selecting the config entry.

## Adding a lock

1. Click **Configure** on the config entry.
2. Add the lock to the **Locks** selector.
3. Submit.

If the new lock already has codes programmed in slots that LCM will manage, a confirmation step lists them before anything is overwritten. Review it carefully — once confirmed, LCM will sync its configured users' PINs onto the lock.

## Removing a lock

1. Click **Configure** on the config entry.
2. Remove the lock from the **Locks** selector.
3. Submit.

LCM removes the entities it created for that lock and unlinks the lock's device from the config entry. The user configuration is untouched and continues to apply to the remaining locks.

> **⚠️ PINs are not cleared from the lock.** Removing a lock only stops LCM from managing it — any codes LCM programmed remain active on the physical lock. If you want them gone, disable the relevant users (or clear their PINs) **first**, wait for the lock to sync, and then remove the lock from the entry.

## Recovering when a lock entity was deleted outside LCM

# External Keypads and Code Readers

Lock Code Manager can check a code entered somewhere it doesn't control — an

conditions you already configured, and record that the credential was used.

Because the check runs against the same users driving your real locks, one PIN
and one schedule cover both. Disable a user and their code stops working at the
keypad too.

Lock Code Manager never opens anything. It answers, records, and fires an event;
what happens next is yours.

## A keypad-only setup needs no lock

Since **5.3.0**, a configuration can manage no locks at all. Create one, leave the
lock picker empty, and add your users and PINs as usual — credentials live in the
configuration, and `use_credential` checks against them. Nothing needs to stand in
for a lock you don't have.

Earlier versions required at least one lock, and the advice was to add a
[Virtual](https://github.com/twrecked/hass-virtual) lock as a placeholder. That is
no longer necessary. An existing entry set up that way keeps working; you can
remove the Virtual lock from it if it was only ever a placeholder.

## The action

```yaml
- action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
  data:
    config_entry_title: House Locks   # or config_entry_id
    code: "{{ entered_code }}"
    source: sensor.keypad_code        # where the code was entered
    target: lock.garage               # what it was used against
  response_variable: check
```

| Response | Value |
|---|---|
| `valid` | `true` / `false` |
| `user` | the user's name when valid, else `null` |
| `reason` | `unknown_code`, `user_disabled`, or `condition_not_met` when invalid |

`source` and `target` are both required and may be any entity — a cover, an
alarm panel, a switch, anything you associate the use with. If you have no natural
entity for one, a template entity works.

Naming the same entity as both is fine, and is what a lock reporting a code used
at its own keypad looks like.

`reason` distinguishes a real-but-inactive credential from an unknown one, and
the action does no rate limiting or logging — so don't wire it to untrusted
input.

## What a valid code produces

**The `lock_code_manager_credential_used` event**, always:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `name` | the user |
| `config_entry_id`, `config_entry_title` | which configuration |
| `source` | where entered |
| `target` | what it was used against |
| `credential_type` | the kind of credential — `pin` today |
| `operation` | what the device did: `lock`, `unlock`, or `unknown` |

`use_credential` always reports `operation: unknown`: it was told a credential was
used, not what happened next, and Lock Code Manager never actuates anything.

The same event fires when one of your locks reports a code used at its own
keypad, so a single trigger covers both.

**The user's `credential_used` event entity**, always. It records every use of
that user's credential whatever the `target` was — a lock, a cover, an alarm
panel, or something Lock Code Manager knows nothing about. The entity stays
available even when every lock in the entry is unreachable, so a use reported
while the locks are down is not lost.

An invalid code produces nothing.

| **Code slot event entity** | The LCM event entity that fires when a PIN is used. | *(required)* |
| **Actions** | HA actions to run when a PIN is used (notifications, scripts, etc.). | *(required)* |
=== Condition Linker ===
| **Lock Code Manager config entry** | The LCM config entry that manages your lock(s). | *(required)* |
| **Slot number** | The code slot number to assign the condition entity to (1–9999). | *(required)* |
| **Condition entity** | The entity to use as the condition. Supports `binary_sensor`, `calendar`, `input_boolean`, `schedule`, and `switch` domains. | *(required)* |

| **Slot number** | The code slot number. Can be a static number or a Jinja2 template using calendar event attributes. | *(required)* |

| **Lock delay (seconds)** | How long to wait after the door closes before locking. Set to 0 to lock immediately. | `5` |

| **Start date/time** | An `input_datetime` helper that defines when the access window begins. | *(required)* |
| **End date/time** | An `input_datetime` helper that defines when the access window ends. | *(required)* |

=== credential_used blueprint description ===
    Runs one or more actions every time a Lock Code Manager credential is
    used, whether Lock Code Manager saw it happen on a lock or was told
    about it through the `lock_code_manager.use_credential` action.


    **Which blueprint should I use?**


    Slot Usage Notifier and Slot Usage Limiter trigger on one user's
    credential used *entity*, so each automation covers the users you point
    it at. All three see the same uses — whether Lock Code Manager watched
    a lock report one or was told about it through
    `lock_code_manager.use_credential`, and whatever the use was against.


    This blueprint triggers on the `lock_code_manager_credential_used`
    event instead, so one automation covers every user in every
    configuration and its filters narrow from there. Reach for the other
    two when you want the focused, per-user recipe; reach for this one when
    you want the whole picture.


    **Available template variables**


    Your actions can reference these variables in templates:

    - `name` — the name of the user whose credential was used

    - `source` — the entity ID where the credential was entered

    - `target` — the entity ID it was used against

Full pass done — all nine blueprints now match their shipped inputs, verified programmatically rather than by eye.

**What the audit turned up beyond the two I'd already fixed:**

- **Credential Used was entirely undocumented.** It ships, and External Keypads told users to "see [[Blueprints]]" for it — a link to a section that didn't exist. - **Calendar PIN Setter** was missing `notify_target`.

The other five (Auto Re-lock, Lock on Door Close, Condition Linker, Date Range, Calendar Condition) were already accurate.

The blueprint says "when PINs are set or cleared" — the opposite situation. I caught it by reading the source instead of trusting the plausible-sounding version, and re-checked the other two `notify_target`/`locks` descriptions the same way; the limiter's and notifier's needed tightening too.

That's the same failure mode as the `lock_entity_ids` understatement earlier in this pass — inventing a specific that reads well. Both are now taken verbatim from the blueprints.

**Wiki state:** two commits, six pages — External Keypads, Virtual integration, Blueprints, Services and Actions, Adding and Removing Locks. Everything checked against released 5.3.0.

content.content:
### Per booking

Change the name to the guest, set a fresh PIN, and let the calendar handle
activation:

```yaml
action: text.set_value
target:
  entity_id: text.all_locks_guest_1_name
data:
  value: Sarah Chen

action: text.set_value
target:
  entity_id: text.all_locks_guest_1_pin
data:
  value: "{{ pin }}"
```

Generate the PIN rather than picking one — [`generate_pin`](Services-and-Actions#generate_pin)
draws from a cryptographic source and rejects sequences, repeats and the
common-leak list:

```yaml
action: lock_code_manager.generate_pin
data:
  length: 6
response_variable: generated

action: text.set_value
target:
  entity_id: text.all_locks_guest_1_pin
data:
  value: "{{ generated.pin }}"
```

Those entity IDs never change, so this automation is written once.

### Fully automated from a calendar

If your booking platform publishes a calendar, the [Calendar PIN
Setter](Blueprints#calendar-pin-setter) blueprint does the whole thing:
extracts a PIN from the event, sets it when the booking starts, clears it when
it ends. Pair it with the [Slot Usage
Notifier](Blueprints#slot-usage-notifier) if you want to know when they first
arrive.

---

## Pattern 2: add and remove per guest

Better when the *count* varies — a contractor for one week, a house-sitter
once a year — and you would otherwise be maintaining standing users who are
empty most of the time. If they are coming back on a schedule, they are
[Pattern 0](#pattern-0-a-permanent-user-on-a-recurring-schedule), not this.

```yaml
action: lock_code_manager.add_user
data:
  config_entry_title: All Locks
  name: Sarah Chen
  pin: "{{ generated.pin }}"
  condition: calendar.bookings
```

and when they leave:

```yaml
action: lock_code_manager.delete_user
data:
  config_entry_title: All Locks
  name: Sarah Chen
```

**Removing a user clears their PIN from every lock in the entry.** That is the
point of removing them. If you want the opposite — hand the code over and stop
tracking it here — pass `clear_credentials: false`, but understand that the
code keeps working and the slot stays occupied.

You do not choose a slot number. Lock Code Manager reads what the locks hold
and allocates a free one, so a slot freed by a departing guest is available to
the next.

Both actions accept `config_entry_title` as well as `config_entry_id`, which
makes hand-written automations readable.

---

## Keeping guests apart from household codes

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("Managing-Guests-and-Rentals.md"); s = p.read_text()

RECIPES = '''---

# Recipes

Complete automations, not fragments — paste one in and change the names. Every
one of them generates the PIN rather than choosing it, because
[`generate_pin`](Services-and-Actions#generate_pin) draws from a cryptographic
source and rejects sequences, repeats and the common-leak list.

## 1. A booking calendar that adds and removes the guest itself

The whole of Pattern 2, driven by the calendar. Two automations: one when a
booking starts, one when it ends.

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Guests: add on booking start"
    triggers:
      - trigger: calendar
        entity_id: calendar.bookings
        event: start
    actions:
      - action: lock_code_manager.generate_pin
        data: {length: 6}
        response_variable: generated
      - action: lock_code_manager.add_user
        data:
          config_entry_title: All Locks
          name: "{{ trigger.calendar_event.summary }}"
          pin: "{{ generated.pin }}"
      - action: notify.send_message
        target:
          entity_id: notify.mobile_app_phone
        data:
          message: >-
            {{ trigger.calendar_event.summary }} arrives today.
            Code {{ generated.pin }}.

  - alias: "Guests: remove on booking end"
    triggers:
      - trigger: calendar
        entity_id: calendar.bookings
        event: end
    actions:
      - action: lock_code_manager.delete_user
        data:
          config_entry_title: All Locks
          name: "{{ trigger.calendar_event.summary }}"
```

The guest's name comes from the event summary, so the two automations agree
about who to remove without storing anything.

> **The summary has to be a usable name and the same one both times.** An event
> titled `Sarah Chen — 3 nights` adds a user under that whole string, and
> renaming the event mid-stay means the remove step names somebody who isn't
> there. If your booking platform writes noisy summaries, either extract the
> name with a template or use [Pattern 1](#pattern-1-rotate-a-standing-user-recommended-for-rentals),
> where the user already exists and only the name and PIN change.

If you would rather the code stop working at checkout **without** removing the
user, pass `condition: calendar.bookings` to `add_user` and drop the second
automation — the condition entity turns the code off when the event ends. The
user stays, holding an inactive code, until you remove them.

## 2. An ad-hoc guest, on demand

For the friend staying this weekend, where there is no calendar. A script with
a field, so it takes one tap from a dashboard button.

```yaml
script:
  add_guest:
    alias: Add a guest code
    fields:
      guest_name:
        name: Guest name
        required: true
        selector:
          text:
    sequence:
      - action: lock_code_manager.generate_pin
        data: {length: 6}
        response_variable: generated
      - action: lock_code_manager.add_user
        data:
          config_entry_title: All Locks
          name: "{{ guest_name }}"
          pin: "{{ generated.pin }}"
      - action: notify.send_message
        target:
          entity_id: notify.mobile_app_phone
        data:
          message: "{{ guest_name }}: {{ generated.pin }}"
```

Removing them is `lock_code_manager.delete_user` with the same name — worth a
second script if you hand out codes often.

## 3. A code good for a fixed number of entries

`add_user` allocates the slot and **waits for the user's entities to exist**
before it returns, so the next step can address them directly.

```yaml
script:
  add_one_use_guest:
    sequence:
      - action: lock_code_manager.generate_pin
        data: {length: 6}
        response_variable: generated
      - action: lock_code_manager.add_user
        data:
          config_entry_title: All Locks
          name: Courier
          pin: "{{ generated.pin }}"
      # The entities now exist, named after the user.
      - action: input_number.set_value
        target:
          entity_id: input_number.courier_uses
        data:
          value: 1
```

Then point the [Slot Usage Limiter](Blueprints#slot-usage-limiter) blueprint at
`event.all_locks_courier_credential_used`, the `enabled` switch, and that
counter. The code disables itself after one entry.

> **Entity IDs come from the name.** A user called `Courier` gets
> `event.all_locks_courier_credential_used`; `Sarah Chen` gets
> `..._sarah_chen_...`. That is fine for a fixed role like `Courier`, which is
> why this recipe uses one — a blueprint automation cannot repoint itself at a
> new entity ID per guest. For rotating guests, keep the standing user of
> [Pattern 1](#pattern-1-rotate-a-standing-user-recommended-for-rentals) and
> rename it: the entity IDs never move, so the limiter stays pointed at the
> same ones.

## Things these share

- **`enabled` defaults to true, and an enabled user must have a PIN.** Adding
  one without a `pin` fails with `'Name' cannot be enabled without a PIN`. Pass
  `enabled: false` to park a user with no code.
- **Names are unique by person, not by spelling.** Two names that normalize to
  the same identity are refused with `A user named 'X' already exists`.
- **You never choose a slot number.** Lock Code Manager reads what the locks
  hold and allocates a free one, so a slot a departing guest freed goes to the
  next arrival.
- **`delete_user` clears the PIN from every lock** unless you pass
  `clear_credentials: false` — which leaves the code working on the lock and
  the slot occupied.
- **PIN length must satisfy your strictest lock.** `generate_pin` takes 4–12
  digits; if a lock takes only 4, ask for 4.

'''

s = s.replace("## Keeping guests apart from household codes", RECIPES + "## Keeping guests apart from household codes")
p.write_text(s)
print("recipes added")

content.text:
Yes — `Managing-Guests-and-Rentals.md` already had three patterns and used both actions, but as **fragments, not runnable automations**. Notably, Pattern 2's `add_user` snippet referenced `{{ generated.pin }}` with no `generate_pin` call in it — copy that and you get an undefined variable. Fixed, and added a **Recipes** section of complete, paste-able automations:

1. **Booking calendar adds and removes the guest itself** — the calendar trigger drives `generate_pin` → `add_user`, and a second automation deletes on event end. The guest's name comes from the event summary so both automations agree without storing anything. With the caveat that matters: if your platform writes summaries like `Sarah Chen — 3 nights`, that whole string becomes the user, and renaming the event mid-stay breaks the removal.
2. **Ad-hoc guest on demand** — a script with a `guest_name` field, one tap from a dashboard button, notifies you the code.
3. **A code good for N entries** — `add_user` then set the counter, pointed at the Slot Usage Limiter.

Recipe 3 is where the interesting constraint lives, and it's why I wrote it around a fixed role (`Courier`) rather than a guest: **entity IDs derive from the user's name**, so a blueprint automation can't repoint itself per guest. That's the concrete argument for Pattern 1's standing-user-plus-rename approach, which the page recommends but didn't previously justify this way.

Everything's verified against the shipped schemas — `generate_pin` is 4–12, `delete_user` clears credentials by default, an enabled user must have a PIN, names are unique by identity not spelling.

**One correction I made to myself:** I first wrote that `add_user` "waits for the user's entities to exist." The code's own docstring is more careful — it waits on the *entry's* settle event, and notes a concurrent write can release it early. I softened it to match and added the practical implication (don't fire two at once), rather than promising a guarantee the code explicitly doesn't make.

If you want a fourth, the obvious gap is **delivering the code to the guest** — SMS/email rather than a notification to you — but that has real security texture worth deciding deliberately rather than me picking a channel.

# Lock Code Manager Wiki

Welcome to the Lock Code Manager wiki!

## Getting Started

- [[Configuration-Structure]] - YAML configuration format
- [[Migrating-from-keymaster]] - Step-by-step guide for switching from keymaster to LCM

## UI

- [[Add-a-UI-for-lock-code-management]] - Overview and decision guide for the dashboard, strategies, and cards
- [[UI-Strategies]] - Dashboard, view, and section strategies (let LCM generate UI from your config)
- [[Custom-Cards]] - User card and lock-codes card (compose your own dashboard)

## Features

- [[Services-and-Actions]] - All registered actions: set/clear PINs, manage condition entities, generate random PINs
- [[Blueprints]] - Usage limiting, calendar-driven PINs, and more
- [[Tracking-lock-state-change-events]] - Listen for lock events in automations
- [[Using-Condition-Entities]] - Control PIN access with calendars, schedules, and more
- [[Unsupported-Condition-Entity-Integrations]] - Condition entities that don't work with LCM

## Advanced

- [[Advanced-Usage]] - Managing multiple config entries and automation tips

## Development

- [[Development-Guide]] - Architecture overview and dev container setup
- [[Adding-a-Provider]] - Step-by-step guide to add support for a new lock integration
- [[Provider-State-Management]] - Understanding poll vs push modes

## Troubleshooting

- [[Troubleshooting]] - Guidance for diagnosing issues and filing bug reports
- [[Troubleshooting-Debug-Logs]] - How to enable debug logging for LCM
- [[Troubleshooting-Device-Diagnostics]] - How to download diagnostics for your lock device
- [[Troubleshooting-Browser-Console-Logs]] - How to capture browser console logs for frontend issues

## FAQ

- [[PIN-Codes-Visible-in-Activity-Log]] - Why PINs are visible in the device activity log
- [[Why-is-'x'-not-supported?-Will-it-be-supported-in-the-future?]]
- [[Unsupported-Integrations]] - Lock integrations that cannot currently be supported

## Supported Integrations

- [[Akuvox-integration]] - Akuvox smart locks and intercoms
- [[External-Keypads]] - check and record codes entered at ESPHome keypads and other readers
- [[Matter-integration]] - Matter-compatible locks
- [[Schlage-integration]] - Schlage WiFi locks
- [[Virtual-integration]] - Virtual locks: a credential store, and a way to try LCM without a real lock
- [[Z-Wave-integration]] - Z-Wave locks
- [[Z-Wave JS UI (MQTT)|Z-Wave-JS-UI-(MQTT)]] - Z-Wave locks bridged via zwave-js-ui's MQTT gateway
- [[ZHA-integration]] - Zigbee Home Automation locks
- [[Zigbee2MQTT-integration]] - Zigbee2MQTT (MQTT-bridged) locks

# Upgrading to 5.0

Lock Code Manager 5.0 is configured by **user**, not by slot number. The slot
number still exists — locks are built around numbered slots and always will be
— but it is bookkeeping now. What you name, see and address is the person
holding the code.

Upgrading migrates each config entry from version 3 to version 4. **It cannot
be undone from inside the integration.** Downgrading Lock Code Manager will not
convert your configuration back; the only way back is restoring a Home
Assistant backup. Take one before you upgrade.

content.content:
[FEATURE] Replace set_usercode/clear_usercode with credential-typed, config-level actions

`set_usercode` and `clear_usercode` are PIN-shaped and device-level. The provider
layer has been credential-shaped since #1227 (`async_set_credential` /
`async_delete_credential`, taking a `CredentialType`), and #1480 establishes that a
member is a credential store rather than a lock. The service surface has not
followed.

## What replaces them

```yaml
lock_code_manager.set_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name              # the user
  credential_type   # pin, rfid, ...
  value

lock_code_manager.clear_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name
  credential_type
```

The type matters on `clear` because one user can hold a PIN and an RFID tag, and
`async_delete_credential` already addresses a `CredentialRef` rather than a slot.

## Why this is not a rename

`async_set_usercode` calls `lock.async_internal_set_usercode(code_slot, usercode)`
— it writes straight to the device and never touches `EntryConfig`. Two
consequences:

- A code written that way is **not in LCM's config**, so LCM sees it as unmanaged
  and, depending on settings, the sync loop may clear it back out. The action can
  fight the thing that manages the lock.
- It **cannot reach a codeless member** (#1484) at all, because there is no device
  to write to. The credentials for those live only in LCM.

A config-level action has neither problem: it updates the user, and sync pushes
the result to every member of the entry.

It also fills a real gap — there is currently no way to give a user anything but a
PIN, since `add_user` takes `pin`.

## Deprecation

Both old actions are long released. Keep them working for a window, mapped to the
new pair with `credential_type: pin`, and warn. **No device-level escape hatch
survives** — writing a credential LCM does not know about is the footgun this
removes, and anything genuinely needing raw access can call the underlying
integration directly.

Note `hard_refresh_usercodes` is a *read* and is unaffected.

## Scope

- The two new actions, their schemas, `services.yaml`, `strings.json` /
  `translations/en.json`.
- Deprecation shims for the old pair, plus whatever the repo uses to surface a
  deprecation (repair issue or log).

content.text:
Good — the semantics are already settled by existing behavior. `async_request_pin_update` is documented as "the authoritative gate for BOTH ends," and an empty PIN **clears it and disables the slot**. So the new actions should route through that coordinator rather than writing config directly — otherwise they'd skip whitespace stripping, per-lock length validation, and the disable-on-clear side effect, and drift from what the UI does.

One thing genuinely changes the size of this work:

options.description: Ship `set_credential` and `clear_credential`. Leave `set_usercode`/`clear_usercode` exactly as they are, device-level and undeprecated. Smallest reviewable change; deprecation becomes its own PR against the next major, alongside #1504.

options.label: New actions + deprecation warning
options.description: Also log a deprecation warning when the old pair is called, and point at the new ones. Keeps them working and behaving identically. Adds strings and tests, but no behavior change for existing users.

options.label: New actions + remap the old pair onto them
options.description: The old actions become shims that call the new config-level path with `credential_type: pin`. This is a real behavior change: `set_usercode` would stop writing straight to the device and start updating the user, so a code it writes is no longer unmanaged. Closes the footgun but could surprise anyone relying on the raw write.

content.subject: Fix #1491: reauth orphans a dropped lock's credential store
content.description: Reauth calls async_update_entry + async_reload, so a lock swapped out never gets the per-lock removal the options flow does: invoke_lock_removed_handlers, lock_dropped repair deletion, and async_unload_lock(remove_permanently=True). For VirtualLock the store IS the credentials, so a cleartext PIN outlives every entry referencing it. Repro test lands in tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py::TestReauthLockSwap. Fix must SHARE the listener's removal block, not duplicate it — a second path would skip the repair deletion exactly like the sibling-method bug. Note async_unload_lock no-ops when the lock instance is absent (runtime_data.locks.pop -> continue), which matters if the entry failed setup.

def _slot_coordinator_for(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    config_entry_id: str | None,
    config_entry_title: str | None,
) -> SlotEntityCoordinator:
    """
    Return the coordinator for the user ``name`` names in the given entry.

    Matched the way a user is recognized everywhere else -- whitespace
    normalized and casefolded -- so the caller may spell the name the way
    they say it rather than the way it was stored.
    """
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)

    stored = next(
        (known for known in config.users if identity(known) == identity(name)), None
    )
    if stored is None:
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"No user named {name!r} in this config entry")

    # A user with no number holds no credential anywhere: allocation could not
    # place them, and there is no slot to write to or clear.
    if (slot_num := config.assignment.slot(stored)) is None:
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"{stored!r} has not been assigned a slot")

    coordinator = config_entry.runtime_data.slot_coordinators.get(slot_num)
    if coordinator is None:
        raise HomeAssistantError(
            f"{stored!r} occupies slot {slot_num}, which this entry has no "
            "coordinator for. Reload the config entry."
        )
    return coordinator


def _managed_credential_type(credential_type: str) -> CredentialType:
    """
    Return the credential type, refusing kinds this integration cannot write.

    Every member of ``CredentialType`` is accepted by the schema so the
    vocabulary is the providers' rather than this action's, and the ones Lock
    Code Manager cannot yet store are refused here instead -- the caller
    learns that RFID is a real kind that is not supported yet, rather than
    that the word is invalid.
    """
    kind = CredentialType(credential_type)
    if kind not in MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES:
        supported = ", ".join(sorted(MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES))
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            f"Lock Code Manager cannot store a {kind} credential. "
            f"Supported: {supported}"
        )
    return kind


async def async_set_credential(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    *,
    credential_type: str,
    value: str,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Set one of a user's credentials, and let the sync carry it to the locks.

    Addresses the user rather than a lock and a slot number. What that buys
    over ``set_usercode`` is that the credential ends up in the
    configuration: a code written straight to a device is one Lock Code
    Manager does not know about, which the sync may clear back out, and which
    cannot reach a member holding its credentials here rather than on a
    device.

    Routed through the slot's coordinator rather than written to the entry,
    because that is the authoritative gate for a credential write -- it strips
    whitespace and validates the length against every bound lock. Writing the
    configuration directly here would be a second path that skips both.
    """
    _managed_credential_type(credential_type)
    if not value.strip():
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            "A credential must have a value; use clear_credential instead"
        )
    coordinator = _slot_coordinator_for(hass, name, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    await coordinator.async_request_pin_update(value)


async def async_clear_credential(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    *,
    credential_type: str,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Clear one of a user's credentials from the configuration and the locks.

    The type is named rather than assumed because one user may eventually
    hold more than one kind, and clearing their PIN must not take their tag
    with it.

    **This disables the user**, which is the same thing emptying their PIN
    field on the dashboard does: a user with no credential and nothing
    disabled would read as active while holding nothing anybody could
    present.
    """
    _managed_credential_type(credential_type)
    coordinator = _slot_coordinator_for(hass, name, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    await coordinator.async_request_pin_update("")

44	    hass: HomeAssistant, config_entry: ConfigEntry, options: dict[str, Any]
45	) -> None:

47	    Write the entry, and wait for it to have finished reacting.
48	
49	    ``async_update_entry`` schedules the update listener rather than
50	    awaiting it, so without this a service returns before the entities for
51	    the users it changed exist. A script that adds a user and then sets
52	    their PIN through the new text entity would find nothing to set.
53	
54	    Waiting on the entry's settle event rather than on the specific
55	    entities keeps this honest about what it can promise: another write
56	    landing at the same time can release the wait early. That is no worse
57	    than not waiting, which is the alternative.
58	    """
59	    runtime_data = config_entry.runtime_data
60	    runtime_data.settled.clear()
61	    if not hass.config_entries.async_update_entry(config_entry, options=options):
62	        # Nothing changed, so no listener will run and nothing will set the
63	        # event. Waiting here would burn the whole timeout for no reason.
64	        return
65	    try:
66	        async with asyncio.timeout(_SETTLE_TIMEOUT):
67	            await runtime_data.settled.wait()

content.description: Add credential_used.yaml to the automation-blueprint list; add a feature bullet for validating codes entered outside LCM-managed locks. Direction/roadmap stays out.

content.description: Currently documents validate_code as a pure query with no events. Needs use_credential (source/target required), the unified event, and the new blueprint. Staged unpushed until merge.

content.description: #1485, #1486, #1487 — read each description against its actual final diff, not against the agent's report. #1487 especially: title and body predate the operation field, credential-type event_types, and the limiter input.

content.description: Fix agent a55956239d83904a5 is applying the three Important findings (declaration exit, orphan pruning, misleading copy) plus the registryless-entity minor. Run /code-review on 1489 once it commits and pushes.

content.subject: Revert #1492 entity lookup from use_credential
content.description: Revert commit e8fe9b77 on feat/lockless-entries: remove lock_entity_id/member_entity_id input from use_credential. Keep config_entry_id and config_entry_title (both shipped in 5.2.0; removing either is breaking). Also removes the queries.py helper and validation.py additions the commit brought in.

content.subject: Add zero-lock availability guard in entity.py
content.description: _is_available currently returns any() over self.locks, so an entry with no locks makes every entity permanently unavailable. Guard so that an entry with no availability sources is available. Do NOT touch the per-lock override at entity.py:374 — those entities always have a lock.

content.subject: Add optional availability source field
content.description: New CONF_AVAILABILITY_ENTITIES: user-picked entities whose availability gates the entry's entities, so a lock-less entry can still follow its keypad going offline. Needs: const, EntryConfig field (from_mapping/to_dict/empty), unified source set used by _is_available AND both TrackStates call sites AND the _handle_available_state_update filter, config flow user+options steps, strings.json + translations/en.json.

content.subject: Test lock-less entries and availability sources
content.description: E2E: entry with zero locks sets up LOADED, entities live, validate_credential resolves the user, use_credential works by entry title. Availability: no sources -> available; configured source going unavailable -> entities unavailable; source recovering -> available. Mutation-check the guard rather than trusting line coverage.

content.subject: Run full suite and prek, open PR
content.description: Full pytest tests/ (not a subset), prek run --all-files, then open PR against feature/credential-store-model using .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md. Keep the description short. No Breaking Change section unless there is a real one. Then close #1494 and #1489 referencing the replacement.

content.subject: Fix #1491: reauth orphans a dropped lock's credential store
content.description: Reauth calls async_update_entry + async_reload, so a lock swapped out never gets the per-lock removal the options flow does: invoke_lock_removed_handlers, lock_dropped repair deletion, and async_unload_lock(remove_permanently=True). For VirtualLock the store IS the credentials, so a cleartext PIN outlives every entry referencing it. Repro test lands in tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py::TestReauthLockSwap. Fix must SHARE the listener's removal block, not duplicate it — a second path would skip the repair deletion exactly like the sibling-method bug. Note async_unload_lock no-ops when the lock instance is absent (runtime_data.locks.pop -> continue), which matters if the entry failed setup.

content.subject: Add set_credential / clear_credential actions (#1493)
content.description: Config-level, credential-typed actions: config_entry_id/title + name (matched by identity(), i.e. whitespace-normalized + casefolded) + credential_type, plus value for set. Route through SlotEntityCoordinator.async_request_pin_update rather than writing config directly — it is documented as the authoritative gate for both ends and carries whitespace stripping, per-lock length validation, and the disable-on-clear side effect. Gate credential_type on MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES (PIN only today). Also log a deprecation warning from set_usercode/clear_usercode pointing at the new pair, without changing their behavior.

async def test_set_credential_updates_the_user_not_just_the_device(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    The credential lands in the configuration, which is the whole point.

    ``set_usercode`` writes straight to a device, so the code it sets is one
    Lock Code Manager does not know about. This addresses the user, so the
    entry holds it and the sync carries it to every lock.
    """
    entry = lock_code_manager_config_entry
    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_SET_CREDENTIAL,
        {
            "config_entry_id": entry.entry_id,
            CONF_NAME: "test1",
            ATTR_CREDENTIAL_TYPE: "pin",
            ATTR_VALUE: "4321",
        },
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    config = get_entry_config(hass.config_entries.async_get_entry(entry.entry_id))
    assert config.users["test1"][CONF_PIN] == "4321"


async def test_set_credential_matches_a_name_the_way_it_is_said(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """Case and surrounding whitespace do not have to match what was stored."""
    entry = lock_code_manager_config_entry
    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_SET_CREDENTIAL,
        {
            "config_entry_id": entry.entry_id,
            CONF_NAME: "  TEST1 ",
            ATTR_CREDENTIAL_TYPE: "pin",
            ATTR_VALUE: "4321",
        },
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    config = get_entry_config(hass.config_entries.async_get_entry(entry.entry_id))
    # Stored under the name it already had, not re-keyed under what was typed.
    assert config.users["test1"][CONF_PIN] == "4321"


async def test_clear_credential_clears_and_disables(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    Clearing takes the credential and the user's active state together.

    A user with no credential who still read as enabled would be advertised
    as able to get in while holding nothing anybody could present. This is
    the same pairing emptying the PIN field on the dashboard produces.
    """
    entry = lock_code_manager_config_entry
    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_CLEAR_CREDENTIAL,
        {
            "config_entry_title": entry.title,
            CONF_NAME: "test1",
            ATTR_CREDENTIAL_TYPE: "pin",
        },
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    config = get_entry_config(hass.config_entries.async_get_entry(entry.entry_id))
    assert not config.users["test1"][CONF_PIN]
    assert config.users["test1"][CONF_ENABLED] is False


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "service,extra",

content.description: Reauth calls async_update_entry + async_reload, so a lock swapped out never gets the per-lock removal the options flow does: invoke_lock_removed_handlers, lock_dropped repair deletion, and async_unload_lock(remove_permanently=True). For VirtualLock the store IS the credentials, so a cleartext PIN outlives every entry referencing it. Repro test lands in tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py::TestReauthLockSwap. cat > /tmp/pr7.md <<'EOF'
## Proposed change

Two config-level, credential-typed actions:

```yaml
lock_code_manager.set_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name              # matched ignoring case and surrounding whitespace
  credential_type   # pin today
  value

lock_code_manager.clear_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name
  credential_type
```

`set_usercode` and `clear_usercode` are PIN-shaped and device-level — they write straight to a lock slot and never touch the configuration. A code written that way is one Lock Code Manager doesn't know about, so the sync may clear it back out, and it can't reach a member that keeps its credentials here rather than on a device. The new pair names the **user**, so the credential lands in the configuration and syncs to every lock in the entry.

### Routed through the coordinator, not written to the entry

Both call `SlotEntityCoordinator.async_request_pin_update`, which the code documents as "the authoritative gate for BOTH ends". That carries three behaviours a direct config write would silently skip: whitespace stripping, per-lock length validation, and **disabling a user whose credential was cleared** — the same pairing that emptying a PIN on the dashboard produces.

`clear_credential` disabling the user is therefore not a new rule; it's the existing one, reached from a second entrance.

### `credential_type` takes the whole vocabulary

The schema accepts every `CredentialType`, and the handler refuses the ones that can't be stored yet against `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` (PIN only). A caller asking for RFID learns it's a real kind that isn't supported, rather than that the word is invalid — and adding a kind later is a one-line change to the set the code already names as the single source of truth.

### Deprecation

`set_usercode` and `clear_usercode` behave **exactly as before** and now log a warning naming their replacement. No remapping — nothing that currently works changes.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [x] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR is related to issue: #1493

Two guards were deliberately **not** written: an empty-value check (the schema strips then requires ≥1 character, so it can't be reached) and a separate no-coordinator branch (unreachable when the slot map and configuration agree, so it's folded into the no-slot check). Both would have been branches no test could take.

async def async_request_active_toggle(self, enabled: bool) -> None:
        """
        Apply an enabled/disabled toggle requested by the switch entity.

        Disable is unconditional. Enable validates that a PIN exists and
        raises ``PinRequiredError`` if absent (the switch translates
        that into ``HomeAssistantError``). On a successful enable the
        ``pin_required`` repair issue is cleared; failures inside the
        issue registry are logged and do not unwind the write.
        """
        if not enabled:
            self._write_config_fields({CONF_ENABLED: False})
            return

        if not self.pin_value:
            self._safely_raise_pin_required_issue()
            raise PinRequiredError(

        self._write_config_fields({CONF_ENABLED: True})
        try:

        except Exception:

content.subject: Fix #1491: reauth orphans a dropped lock's credential store
content.description: Reauth calls async_update_entry + async_reload, so a lock swapped out never gets the per-lock removal the options flow does: invoke_lock_removed_handlers, lock_dropped repair deletion, and async_unload_lock(remove_permanently=True). For VirtualLock the store IS the credentials, so a cleartext PIN outlives every entry referencing it. Repro test lands in tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py::TestReauthLockSwap. Fix must SHARE the listener's removal block, not duplicate it — a second path would skip the repair deletion exactly like the sibling-method bug. Note async_unload_lock no-ops when the lock instance is absent (runtime_data.locks.pop -> continue), which matters if the entry failed setup.

content.subject: Add set_credential / clear_credential actions (#1493)
content.description: Config-level, credential-typed actions: config_entry_id/title + name (matched by identity(), i.e. whitespace-normalized + casefolded) + credential_type, plus value for set. Route through SlotEntityCoordinator.async_request_pin_update rather than writing config directly — it is documented as the authoritative gate for both ends and carries whitespace stripping, per-lock length validation, and the disable-on-clear side effect. Gate credential_type on MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES (PIN only today). Also log a deprecation warning from set_usercode/clear_usercode pointing at the new pair, without changing their behavior.

async def test_set_credential_leaves_the_user_alone_by_default(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    Giving somebody a credential is not the same as letting them in.

    A user cleared earlier stays off until somebody says otherwise, so a
    credential set on them is present and inert rather than quietly live.
    """
    entry = lock_code_manager_config_entry
    common = {"config_entry_id": entry.entry_id, ATTR_CREDENTIAL_TYPE: "pin"}

    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN, SERVICE_CLEAR_CREDENTIAL, {**common, CONF_NAME: "test1"}, blocking=True
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_SET_CREDENTIAL,
        {**common, CONF_NAME: "test1", ATTR_VALUE: "4321"},
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    config = get_entry_config(hass.config_entries.async_get_entry(entry.entry_id))
    assert config.users["test1"][CONF_PIN] == "4321"
    assert config.users["test1"][CONF_ENABLED] is False


async def test_set_credential_can_enable_in_the_same_call(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
) -> None:
    """
    ``enable`` makes this the inverse of clearing rather than half of it.

    Clearing disables, so without this a caller undoing a clear needs a
    second action against a different entity to finish the job.
    """
    entry = lock_code_manager_config_entry
    common = {"config_entry_id": entry.entry_id, ATTR_CREDENTIAL_TYPE: "pin"}

    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN, SERVICE_CLEAR_CREDENTIAL, {**common, CONF_NAME: "test1"}, blocking=True
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_SET_CREDENTIAL,
        {**common, CONF_NAME: "test1", ATTR_VALUE: "4321", ATTR_ENABLE: True},
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    config = get_entry_config(hass.config_entries.async_get_entry(entry.entry_id))
    assert config.users["test1"][CONF_PIN] == "4321"
    assert config.users["test1"][CONF_ENABLED] is True

content.text:
Added to **#1505**. `set_credential` now takes `enable`, default `false`.

**Why off by default:** clearing disables the user, so without this, setting a credential on someone cleared earlier leaves a code that's present but inert — you'd need a second action against the switch entity to finish. `enable` closes that. But giving someone a credential and letting them in are different decisions, and only the caller knows whether they're making both, so it's opt-in.

**Two implementation choices worth noting:**

I call the coordinator's `async_request_active_toggle(True)` rather than writing `enabled` alongside the PIN. Enabling has its own rules — it refuses a user with no credential, and clears the `pin_required` repair issue raised when that happened. Writing the field directly would skip both, which is the same "second path" trap I avoided on the write side.

**The ordering is load-bearing, and I verified it rather than assumed it.** `async_request_active_toggle(True)` checks `pin_value` before enabling, so the PIN must already be visible. `_write_config_fields` refreshes `runtime_data.config` eagerly after `async_update_entry` — its docstring explicitly flags the trap where a listener hasn't refreshed between two consecutive writes. So PIN-then-enable is safe, and enable-then-PIN would fail. Mutation M3 reverses them and a test catches it.

Named `enable` rather than `enabled` deliberately: it's a verb, so omitting it leaves the user as they were. `enabled: false` would naturally read as "disable them," which isn't what it does.

Verified: 2288 passing, 100% coverage, all hooks green, six mutations killed.

Still outstanding from before: the wiki's Services and Actions page doesn't cover the new pair or the deprecation. Want that now, or once #1505 merges?

content.text: how about enable_if_disabled

Fair — it's more explicit about the one-directional effect, which matters for something access-related. Renaming.

One thing I want to be honest about rather than quietly get wrong: I'm **not** adding a `not is_enabled` guard to match the name literally. Enabling an already-enabled user is already a no-op (`async_update_entry` returns `False` when nothing changed, so no listener runs), so the guard would be an unobservable branch no test could kill — and the name describes the observable effect accurately without it.

37	# How long to wait for the entry to react to a write before returning
38	# anyway. Generous, because the pass can set up a lock it has never
39	# spoken to; a caller stuck here is waiting on that, not on this.
40	_SETTLE_TIMEOUT = 30

43	async def _async_write_and_settle(
44	    hass: HomeAssistant, config_entry: ConfigEntry, options: dict[str, Any]
45	) -> None:
46	    """
47	    Write the entry, and wait for it to have finished reacting.
48	
49	    ``async_update_entry`` schedules the update listener rather than
50	    awaiting it, so without this a service returns before the entities for
51	    the users it changed exist. A script that adds a user and then sets
52	    their PIN through the new text entity would find nothing to set.
53	
54	    Waiting on the entry's settle event rather than on the specific
55	    entities keeps this honest about what it can promise: another write
56	    landing at the same time can release the wait early. That is no worse
57	    than not waiting, which is the alternative.
58	    """
59	    runtime_data = config_entry.runtime_data
60	    runtime_data.settled.clear()
61	    if not hass.config_entries.async_update_entry(config_entry, options=options):
62	        # Nothing changed, so no listener will run and nothing will set the
63	        # event. Waiting here would burn the whole timeout for no reason.
64	        return
65	    try:
66	        async with asyncio.timeout(_SETTLE_TIMEOUT):
67	            await runtime_data.settled.wait()
68	    except TimeoutError:
69	        # The write itself is durable, so this is not a failure to report to
70	        # the caller -- the entities will appear when the pass finishes.
71	        _LOGGER.warning(

73	            "this change may appear late",
74	            config_entry.entry_id,
75	            config_entry.title,

content.text:
Renamed to `enable_if_disabled` across the schema, handler, `services.yaml`, and both strings files. **#1505** updated.

The name is better for the reason you're getting at: it says the effect is one-directional. `enabled: false` would naturally read as "disable them," which this never does.

**What I deliberately didn't do, and said so in the PR:** add a `not is_enabled` guard to make the implementation match the name literally. Enabling someone already enabled is already a no-op — `async_update_entry` returns `False` when the value hasn't changed, so no listener runs and nothing syncs. A conditional would be a branch no test could distinguish from its absence, which is the kind of coverage-proof dead code I've been pulling out of this codebase all session. The name describes the observable effect accurately as-is.

Verified after the rename: 2288 passing, 100% coverage, strings and `en.json` byte-identical, all hooks green.

**Final shape of #1505:**

```yaml
lock_code_manager.set_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name                # matched ignoring case and whitespace
  credential_type     # pin today
  value
  enable_if_disabled  # optional, default false

lock_code_manager.clear_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name
  credential_type
```

Six mutations killed, including the ordering one — enabling before the PIN write fails, because the enable path checks that a credential exists.

Still open: the wiki's Services and Actions page needs the new pair and the deprecation. Say the word once this merges.

content.content:
## set_usercode

Write a PIN to a specific slot on a lock that LCM is currently managing. This goes through LCM's internal write path, so it respects the same rate limits, sync bookkeeping, and provider routing as the normal slot-driven flow — but **does not change the slot's configured PIN**. The next time the sync manager reconciles the slot, the configured PIN will be re-applied.

This is primarily useful for one-off automation needs (e.g. temporarily writing a PIN that an external system generated). For persistent codes, edit the slot's PIN entity instead.

| Field | Required | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lock_entity_id` | yes | lock entity | The lock to write the PIN on. Must be managed by an LCM config entry. |
| `code_slot` | yes | int | Target slot number on the lock. |
| `usercode` | yes | string | The PIN to write. Cannot be empty or whitespace. |

**Errors:** `ServiceValidationError` if the lock isn't managed by any LCM config entry.

```yaml
action: lock_code_manager.set_usercode
data:
  lock_entity_id: lock.front_door
  code_slot: 3
  usercode: "9482"
```

---

## clear_usercode

input.command:
cd /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager.wiki
/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("Services-and-Actions.md"); s = p.read_text()

DEPRECATION = """
> **Deprecated — use [`set_credential`](#set_credential) instead.** This writes straight to a device, so the code it sets is one Lock Code Manager does not know about: the sync may clear it back out, and it cannot reach a member whose credentials live here rather than on a lock. It still works and now logs a warning naming its replacement. It will be removed in a future major version.
"""
DEPRECATION_CLEAR = DEPRECATION.replace("[`set_credential`](#set_credential)", "[`clear_credential`](#clear_credential)").replace("the code it sets is one Lock Code Manager does not know about: the sync may clear it back out, and it", "it clears a slot without telling the configuration, so the sync may write the code straight back. It")

s = s.replace("""## set_usercode

Write a PIN to a specific slot""", """## set_usercode
""" + DEPRECATION + """
Write a PIN to a specific slot""")

s = s.replace("""## clear_usercode
""", """## clear_usercode
""" + DEPRECATION_CLEAR, 1)

NEW = """## set_credential

Set one of a person's credentials in a config entry. Unlike [`set_usercode`](#set_usercode), this addresses the **user**, and the credential lands in the configuration — so it is synced to every lock in the entry and managed like any other, rather than looking like a code somebody programmed by hand.

The name is matched the way a user is recognised everywhere else: ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. `"  sarah chen "` finds `Sarah Chen`.

| Field | Required | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `config_entry_id` | one of | string | The config entry the person belongs to. |
| `config_entry_title` | one of | string | The same entry, named by its title. |
| `name` | yes | string | The person. Matched ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. |
| `credential_type` | yes | select | Which kind. Only `pin` can be stored today; the others are refused with a message saying so. |
| `value` | yes | string | The credential itself. Surrounding whitespace is stripped. |
| `enable_if_disabled` | no | boolean | Turn the person on once the credential is set. Defaults to `false`. Never disables anybody. |

**Errors:** `ServiceValidationError` if no user of that name is in the entry, if they hold no slot, or if the credential type is one Lock Code Manager cannot store.

```yaml
action: lock_code_manager.set_credential
data:
  config_entry_title: All Locks
  name: Sarah Chen
  credential_type: pin
  value: "9482"
  enable_if_disabled: true
```

> **Why `enable_if_disabled` is off by default.** Clearing a credential disables the person, so setting one on somebody cleared earlier would otherwise leave a code that is present but inert. Giving a user a credential and letting them in are different decisions, so you have to ask for the second one.

---

## clear_credential

Remove one of a person's credentials from the configuration and from every lock in the entry.

**This also disables the person** — the same thing emptying their PIN on the dashboard does. A user with no credential who still read as enabled would be advertised as able to get in while holding nothing anybody could present.

The credential type is named rather than assumed because one person may eventually hold more than one kind, and clearing a PIN must not take a tag with it.

| Field | Required | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `config_entry_id` | one of | string | The config entry the person belongs to. |
| `config_entry_title` | one of | string | The same entry, named by its title. |
| `name` | yes | string | The person. Matched ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. |
| `credential_type` | yes | select | Which kind to clear. |

```yaml
action: lock_code_manager.clear_credential
data:
  config_entry_title: All Locks
  name: Sarah Chen
  credential_type: pin
```

To remove the person entirely rather than just their credential, use [`delete_user`](#delete_user).

---

## set_usercode"""
s = s.replace("## set_usercode", NEW, 1)
p.write_text(s)
print("page updated")
PY
grep -n "^## " Services-and-Actions.md

```yaml
lock_code_manager.enable_user:
```

The last writable per-user surface the UI had and the actions didn't. What the dashboard exposes per person is their **name**, **PIN** and **enabled** state; `set_credential` covered the PIN, and this covers the switch.

**Addressed by name, not entity ID** — which is the point rather than a convenience. Entity IDs derive from the user's name, so `switch.all_locks_sarah_chen_enabled` moves the moment somebody is renamed, and an automation holding it silently stops working. A name survives that.

**Disable** is unconditional (there's no state that makes turning somebody off invalid) and **keeps the credential in the configuration**, so enabling them again restores it without anybody having to remember what it was.
